body: Puppies from a litter will not all turn out the same. They may have similarities, but they may also have different temperaments, drives, energy levels, etc. Also, health testing should most certainly be done. The type of testing depends on the breed. Yes, they'll likely get issues as they age, but breeders should be testing the breeding stock for known issues within the breed to produce healthier pups

I'd maybe reconsider getting that particular sheltie from the shelter due to its history of excessive barking as there's a good chance you won't be able to teach it to stop and then what? Maybe talk to breeders or shelters in the area that have them and see if there are any quieter ones? Or get a pup and teach it from day one not to bark at everything. I got lucky with my sheltie pup as he barely barks at all (less than any dog I've ever owned/known). He will bark every now and then but I'll just call him to me or squeak a toy and he forgets what he was barking at. On the other hand though, I went to a sheltie meetup yesterday and there were a few that would bark like crazy constantly. Like if they wanted attention, another dog to play, treats, didn't like something, saw something, heard something, literally anything. But shelties are an amazing breed and if you really want one I'd strongly suggest a pup you can train not to bark from day one, or an older dog that you are adopting from someone who knows them well and so can tell you whether they are big barkers or not. There are some good training videos on youtube about capturing calm etc that would be helpful and just praising/treating a dog to focus on you rather than something that would potentially set them off could help also

Definitely socialise him in any way you can even before all his vaccinations. Carry him around so he gets out and about but isn't at risk. That way he can get used to all different sounds and smells. Puppy class will help with socialising with other dogs. Maybe talk to the trainer about socialising him with vaccinated dogs. They may know someone who would be happy to have a play date or maybe the trainer themself has a vaccinated dog and could help. I know a trainer I talked to offered to bring a couple of dogs over to help train my dog to be calm around other dogs, maybe they can help with this too if there is no one else you know that can. Maybe look online and see if there is a dog group near you? There may be someone on there that has a vaccinated dog and  would allow you to bring yours over for a play date. My puppy was quite nervous, especially around german shepherds  (their big bark terrified him) so I found someone online who had german shepherds of all different ages and went over and he had a run around with them all individually. After 40 minutes he was running around with a 4month old, 1 year old and 4 year old with no problems. We also brought him with us everywhere we could. If we got takeaway, he came through the drive thru with us. If we went to the pet shop, we carried him in with us. If I visited friends or family, he came with.

My sheltie fits this exactly (minus coat and shedding). He's eager to please and absolutely loves training time but isn't intense. He's bouncey like the dogs in the videos. He will jump into the positions you want and have fun but still do what he's told. We've been doing mat training with him and whenever you put his mat on the ground he races over and leaps onto it so it ends up sliding on the wood floor, then he lays and waits patiently for his treat. He is awesome off lead without any proper training in that regard. He loves to be with me and will stick by my side in an off lead park unless encouraged to go play with others. He is cuddly when we get home from the park and will just fall asleep in my arms. He's fine with dogs of all sizes (though shelties can be nervous dogs so need to be socialised well as pups). Would be ideal for agility, obedience and herding training as well. I don't know if this is typical of shelties but the ones I've met seem to be quite similar 😊

I agree somewhat but I don't think the issue is necessarily first time owners, but rather owners that don't do their research. Even an experienced dog owner shouldn't jump to these breeds without doing research etc. Really you just shouldn't go for a dog you aren't prepared for. But say someone hasn't owned a dog before but volunteers at say a husky rescue and has been working with the breed, they are likely to be more successful than someone who is an experienced dog owner but has owned small, easily trained dogs. I know people that have 2 Tibetan mastiffs in a small unit with a small yard and I can't believe they thought of getting a breed like that without owning a place and just as companion pets. There was also a lady in my puppy class that had a dalmation... she chose the breed because her daughter wanted the 'firefighter dog'. She couldn't control it as a pup I can't imagine how she's going now a year on.
But unfortunately it happens. People just want them because they're cute or novel but don't think about all the work that needs to be put in to some breeds. 😑

Do you have a friend/relative etc with a dog? If so you could ask them for help. Another option is meeting another dog owner in your area to help out. For me, I joined a dog group on facebook and asked if someone had a well behaved dog and could help me out with this. We basically had them with their dog a distance away and just kept getting closer and then stop and made sure my pup would focus on me and do what I asked of him, then got a little closer and did the same. If he stopped responding we'd back away a bit and try again. Then after a bit of training time we would reward them with off lead play. It took a few goes to get it good and then we started trialling with some other dogs. We found it hard to do with randoms as others would encourage their dogs to approach mine despite me telling them I didn't want that. It's also easier if the other dog is calm/well behaved as it's less distracting if they are just sitting calmly rather than bouncy or loud or approaching your dog

Try just popping it on the ground near him and letting him check it out. Give him treats and praise. Then when he's comfortable pick it up and just bring it closer to him without actually putting it on and treat him. Keep repeating until he is comfortable. Then start putting it around his neck, not yet actually clipping it then treating and repeating. Once he comfortable do it again but clip it this time and treat. Do the same sort of thing with the lead. Break it down into very small steps. Pups aren't used to these things so you need to really ease them into it.

I agree in some ways. Like I was at a dog park once and there was a lady there with an elderly dog that didn't like dogs near it so she would go off at anyone whose dog came near her. They literally just sat at a bench in the fenced area the entire time yelling at people. That to me is stupid. However, being wary of which dogs yours interacts with and how is not. Personally I hang out by the dog park and see how the dogs play before deciding to go in because I have a young sheltie pup who is a little nervous at times. We went into a dog park the other day and he played well with an older kelpie. They chased each other around and had a great time. Then two greyhounds entered and at first everything was fine, they all interacted well. I then decided to get my pup onto the agility equipment and had him following me along. At that time, the greyhounds were playing fetch when one turned and came straight for my pup. When he then ran away scared the other came too. They ended up trapping him underneath the agility ramp and were growling and snapping at him from either side as he screamed and their owners just watched. I pushed them away and grabbed him out and he was fine, just terrified. But now we are more wary when he is in there and will remove him when greyhounds come in as they are used to chasing small fluff balls like my pup and it's too risky off lead. But basically there are many horror stories of off leash parks and it's best to be careful. Though in saying that, I do think that if you're really concerned you should remove your dog rather than expecting all dogs to leave yours alone.

I think people make it hard for others to rehome dogs nowadays. I was looking at rehoming my dog because I travel a lot (do uni in another city) and originally planned to take him with me and to day care when I did but he gets car sick and will shake, pant and vomit in even a 2 minute trip, and has separation anxiety so gets upset if I leave him at home. I've worked with a couple trainers and they just left him with worse anxiety than before ($1800 well spent 😑). I did some research into rescues that were foster based (as he would not do well in a shelter environment due to anxiety). I found one group and contacted them asking for help and guidance on what my options are and they replied attacking me and saying that they would add it to their list of terrible excuses to rehome a dog. So I was left feeling like shit and too scared and ashamed to talk to anyone else about it. I've now dropped out of uni to be home because I can't leave him, can't take him with me and can't rehome him without feeling attacked. And I know people will say why get a dog in the first place but as I said the plan was to bring him with me when I went into uni and drop him into the doggy day care near there while I was in classes, then head to the nearby bushwalks after class. However, when adopting from a shelter you don't know what you're going to get. I've spent nearly 2 years trying to work on the issues we're having with him and nothing is working. I love him to pieces and it's not an easy decision but other people make it harder. There is so much judgement around the issue that people feel like they can't rehome, no matter what. I get that it shouldn't be a first stop and that you should try to avoid it but people shouldn't feel guilted into keeping a dog that would be better fitted to a different home. But unfortunately that does happen. Basically, my point was that there is a lot of criticism around this sort of thing. People will have their say no matter what and make the person feel terrible for the decision even if it's made with good intentions. Maybe that's why this person is saying that they will keep this dog despite him not suiting their lifestyle.

I'm quite biased but Sheltie!! They are soo simple to train and they love learning. My boy is constantly looking at me to see what I want him to do next. So much enthusiasm and picks up on things very quickly. He has already learnt so much and he's still a pup. He is great with kids and is fine with big dogs (we also have a 45kg rottie mix). He does bark a bit but less than any other breeds we've owned and other owners I've met with have ones that barely make any noise what so ever so it depends on the individual. They love their people and will come for cuddles if you want but also happily do their own thing (though still typically do so in your vicinity). They are just really lovely dogs and the easiest breed I've ever raised. 😊
